definition: The foundational teaching of Buddhism: suffering exists, suffering has a cause (craving), suffering can cease, and there is a path to cessation. This framework forms the basis of Buddhist soteriology.
The path to liberation consisting of right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and concentration. It represents the practical method for ending suffering.
The principle that all phenomena arise in dependence upon causes and conditions, with nothing existing independently. Central to Buddhist ontology and the understanding of causality.
The absence of inherent existence or intrinsic nature in all phenomena. A core Mahayana doctrine particularly emphasized in Madhyamaka philosophy.
The constant change and transience of all conditioned phenomena. One of the three marks of existence.
Existential dissatisfaction, stress, or unsatisfactoriness inherent in conditioned existence. The first noble truth and one of the three marks of existence.
The absence of a permanent, unchanging self or soul in persons and phenomena. The third mark of existence and a distinctive Buddhist teaching.
The cessation of suffering and liberation from cyclic existence achieved through the elimination of ignorance, craving, and aversion. The ultimate goal in Buddhist practice.
The cycle of birth, death, and rebirth characterized by suffering and driven by karma and mental afflictions. The state from which liberation is sought.
Intentional action that produces consequences affecting future experiences and rebirths. The ethical principle of cause and effect governing existence.
The three characteristics shared by all conditioned phenomena: impermanence, suffering, and non-self. Understanding these is essential to awakening.
The five components of experience: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Buddhist analysis shows these contain no permanent self.
The twelve interdependent factors that perpetuate cyclic existence, from ignorance through aging and death. A detailed elaboration of dependent origination.
The path between extremes of self-indulgence and self-mortification, and philosophically, between eternalism and nihilism. A core Buddhist principle.

term_tibetan: de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po
definition: The inherent potential for awakening present in all sentient beings. A key Mahayana teaching emphasizing the positive basis for liberation.
The mind of awakening or aspiration to achieve buddhahood for the benefit of all beings. The foundation of the Mahayana path.
Penetrating insight into the true nature of reality, especially emptiness and dependent origination. One of the six perfections and essential for liberation.
The wish for all beings to be free from suffering and its causes. Central to Mahayana ethics and the bodhisattva path.
Adaptive teaching methods suited to the capacities and needs of different beings. A key Mahayana concept explaining diversity in Buddhist teachings.
The three dimensions of buddhahood: truth body (dharmakaya), enjoyment body (sambhogakaya), and emanation body (nirmanakaya). A Mahayana doctrine of Buddha's nature.
The distinction between conventional/relative truth and ultimate truth. A fundamental hermeneutical framework in Mahayana philosophy.
Buddha (awakened teacher), Dharma (teachings), and Sangha (community) as the objects of refuge. The foundation of Buddhist commitment.
The root mental afflictions of greed/attachment, hatred/aversion, and ignorance/delusion. These perpetuate suffering and bind beings to samsara.
Mental cultivation through concentrated attention and contemplation. The primary method for developing insight and liberation in Buddhism.
The development of stable, one-pointed concentration free from distraction. Forms the foundation for insight meditation.
Analytical meditation cultivating direct perception of impermanence, suffering, and non-self. The wisdom component that leads to liberation.
Seated meditation practice in Zen Buddhism, often characterized by objectless awareness and non-discursive presence. The core practice of Zen tradition.
Tibetan Buddhist contemplative system emphasizing the natural, primordial state of mind. The highest teaching in Nyingma tradition.
Meditation system pointing to the ultimate nature of mind as luminous and empty. A key practice in Kagyu and other Tibetan traditions.
Meditation practice of visualizing taking others' suffering and giving one's own happiness. A method for developing compassion in Tibetan Buddhism.
The cultivation of unconditional friendliness and benevolence toward all beings. One of the four immeasurables and a central meditation practice.
Present-moment awareness and retention of attention on meditation objects or activities. A crucial factor in the path to awakening.
Deep states of meditative concentration characterized by unification of mind and stability. Essential for developing insight.
The Middle Way philosophical school founded by Nagarjuna, emphasizing emptiness and freedom from conceptual extremes. One of two major Mahayana philosophical systems.
Mahayana school emphasizing consciousness and mental phenomena, teaching that experience is constructed by mind. Founded by Asanga and Vasubandhu.
Systematic philosophical and psychological analysis of Buddhist teachings. Forms the third basket of the Buddhist canon.
Four-cornered logical system examining propositions as true, false, both, or neither. Used in Madhyamaka to deconstruct conceptual reification.
Madhyamaka sub-school that refutes opponents' positions through reductio ad absurdum without asserting positive theses. Associated with Candrakirti and Tibetan Gelug tradition.
The notion of intrinsic, independent nature that Madhyamaka philosophy refutes as the basis of emptiness. The target of ultimate analysis.
Abhidharma analysis of reality into irreducible momentary constituents. A pluralist ontology contrasting with Madhyamaka emptiness.
The doctrine that all conditioned phenomena exist only for an instant before ceasing. An Abhidharma teaching on radical impermanence.
Afflictive obscurations preventing liberation and cognitive obscurations preventing omniscience. Removing both achieves full buddhahood.
Yogacara teaching distinguishing imagined nature, dependent nature, and perfected nature. A framework for understanding reality and delusion.
Moral discipline and restraint from harmful actions forming the foundation of Buddhist practice. One of the three trainings.
Basic ethical guidelines for lay Buddhists: refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxication. The foundation of Buddhist lay ethics.

term_tibetan: byang chub sems dpa'i sdom pa
definition: The commitment to achieve buddhahood for the benefit of all beings. The ethical foundation of Mahayana practice.
The body of rules governing monastic life and conduct. One of the three baskets of Buddhist scripture.
The principle of non-violence and avoiding harm to living beings. A foundational Buddhist ethical value.
Earning a living through ethical means that don't harm others. The fifth factor of the Noble Eightfold Path.
The fundamental aspect of consciousness that cognizes objects and can be cultivated toward awakening. Subject of extensive Buddhist psychological analysis.
The thinking faculty or mental sense that processes information and generates thought. The sixth sense base in Buddhist psychology.
The foundational level of consciousness that stores karmic seeds and underlies experience. A key Yogacara concept explaining continuity.
Mental states that arise with and qualify consciousness, including feeling, perception, attention, and volition. Abhidharma enumerates fifty-two or more.
Disturbing emotions and attitudes that cause suffering and perpetuate cyclic existence. The primary obstacles to liberation.
Volitional mental activities and karmic formations. The fourth aggregate and second link of dependent origination.
Awareness that discerns objects through the six sense faculties. The fifth aggregate analyzed into multiple types in Abhidharma and Yogacara.
First stage of awakening, having entered the stream to nirvana and eliminated doubt, attachment to rites, and view of self. Assured of at most seven more rebirths.
Second stage of awakening, having greatly weakened sensual desire and aversion. Will be reborn in the human realm at most once more.
Third stage of awakening, having eliminated sensual desire and aversion. Will not return to the human realm but attain nirvana in a higher rebirth.
One who has achieved liberation from cyclic existence through eliminating all afflictions and ignorance. The fourth and final stage in the Theravada path.
A being committed to achieving full buddhahood for the benefit of all beings. The ideal practitioner in Mahayana Buddhism.
One who achieves awakening independently without a teacher and doesn't teach others extensively. Considered superior to arhats but inferior to full buddhas.
The ten progressive stages of bodhisattva development from first bhumi to near-buddhahood. Each stage is characterized by perfection of specific virtues.
The five progressive stages of spiritual development: accumulation, preparation, seeing, meditation, and no-more-learning. A systematic outline of the path in Mahayana.
The dissolution of the physical body into light at death, leaving only hair and nails. A sign of realization in Dzogchen and tantric practice.
The realms of rebirth in samsara: hell beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, demigods, and gods. Each realm characterized by particular sufferings.
The three levels of cyclic existence: desire realm, form realm, and formless realm. A cosmological framework for understanding rebirth states.
An immeasurably long period of cosmic time in which worlds form and dissolve. Used to indicate vast temporal scales in Buddhist cosmology.
The cosmic mountain at the center of Buddhist cosmology, surrounded by continents and oceans. The axis mundi of traditional Buddhist world-systems.
Buddha-fields free from suffering where beings can easily practice toward liberation. Particularly associated with Amitabha Buddha's western paradise.
The historical Buddha, Siddhartha Gautama, who lived in ancient India and founded Buddhism. The sage of the Shakya clan.
Second-century Indian philosopher who founded the Madhyamaka school and systematized the teaching of emptiness. One of the most influential Buddhist thinkers.
Fourth-century Indian philosopher who contributed to both Abhidharma and Yogacara traditions. Brother of Asanga and author of important commentaries.
Fourteenth-century Tibetan master who founded the Gelug tradition and wrote extensive commentaries on sutra and tantra. Major reformer of Tibetan Buddhism.
Thirteenth-century Japanese master who founded Soto Zen and emphasized shikantaza (just sitting). Author of the Shobogenzo.
Semi-legendary Indian monk who brought Chan/Zen Buddhism to China in the sixth century. Credited as the first patriarch of Chan.
Eighth-century Indian tantric master who established Buddhism in Tibet. Revered as the second Buddha in Nyingma tradition.
Fourth-century Indian philosopher who founded the Yogacara school. Traditionally said to have received teachings from Maitreya.
Eleventh-century Tibetan yogi and poet who achieved enlightenment in one lifetime. Famous for his songs and devotion to his teacher Marpa.
Eleventh-century Indian master who revitalized Buddhism in Tibet and wrote the influential Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment. Founder of the Kadam tradition.
Buddhist scriptures recording the Buddha's teachings. The second basket of the Buddhist canon containing doctrinal and narrative material.
Esoteric Buddhist texts teaching advanced meditation and ritual practices. The scriptural basis for Vajrayana Buddhism.
Commentarial and philosophical works by later masters explicating Buddhist teachings. Distinguished from sutras as human rather than Buddha's word.
Concise Mahayana text teaching emptiness through the dialog between Avalokiteshvara and Shariputra. One of the most widely recited Buddhist texts.
Mahayana perfection of wisdom text teaching non-attachment and emptiness. Known for the phrase about phenomena being like dreams and bubbles.
Influential Mahayana text teaching one vehicle, eternal Buddha, and universal buddha-nature. Central to East Asian Buddhism.
Genre of Mahayana sutras teaching emptiness and the bodhisattva path. Includes texts from brief Heart Sutra to massive 100,000-verse versions.
Mahayana text teaching Yogacara doctrines including storehouse consciousness. Important in Chan/Zen tradition.
Teaching attributed to Huineng, the sixth Chan patriarch, emphasizing sudden enlightenment. The only Chinese text called a sutra.
The Buddhist community, particularly the monastic order. One of the three jewels of refuge.
A residential community for Buddhist monastics dedicated to practice, study, and teaching. The institutional center of Buddhist tradition.

term_tibetan: pha rol tu phyin pa drug
definition: The six virtues cultivated by bodhisattvas: generosity, ethics, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom. The framework of Mahayana practice.
The practice of giving material goods, teachings, or fearlessness. The first perfection and foundation of merit accumulation.
Tolerance of harm, acceptance of suffering, and certainty in the teachings. The third perfection essential for bodhisattva practice.
Enthusiastic perseverance and joyful effort in virtue. The fourth perfection necessary for completing the path.
Loving-kindness, compassion, empathetic joy, and equanimity cultivated toward all beings. Key meditations for developing altruism.
Rejoicing in others' happiness and success without envy. The third immeasurable complementing compassion.
Impartial balance free from attachment and aversion. The fourth immeasurable that stabilizes the other three.

term_en: Four Noble Truths of the Path
definition: The fourth noble truth: the path leading to cessation of suffering, specifically the Noble Eightfold Path. The practical method of liberation.
The third noble truth: cessation of suffering is possible through eliminating craving. The goal of Buddhist practice.
The second noble truth: suffering originates from craving, aversion, and ignorance. The diagnosis of the problem.
Compulsive desire and thirst for pleasure, existence, or non-existence. The primary cause of suffering in the second noble truth.
Fundamental misapprehension of reality, particularly regarding impermanence, suffering, and non-self. The root cause of cyclic existence.
Clinging to sensual pleasures, views, rules, or self-doctrine. The ninth link in dependent origination intensifying craving.
The process of coming into existence or the karma that propels rebirth. The tenth link in dependent origination.
The arising of the aggregates in a new life. The eleventh link in dependent origination following becoming.
The inevitable decay and cessation of life. The twelfth and final link in dependent origination representing suffering's culmination.
The meeting of sense faculty, object, and consciousness. The sixth link in dependent origination that produces feeling.
The hedonic tone of experience as pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral. The second aggregate and seventh link in dependent origination.
Recognition and interpretation of sensory data through concepts. The third of the five aggregates.
Material form including the physical body and sense objects. The first of the five aggregates.
Correct understanding of the four noble truths and dependent origination. The first factor of the Noble Eightfold Path.
Thoughts of renunciation, good will, and harmlessness. The second factor of the Noble Eightfold Path.
Abstaining from false, divisive, harsh, and idle speech. The third factor of the Noble Eightfold Path.

term_tibetan: yang dag pa'i las kyi mtha'
definition: Abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. The fourth factor of the Noble Eightfold Path.
Cultivation of wholesome states and abandonment of unwholesome ones. The sixth factor of the Noble Eightfold Path.
Continuous awareness of body, feelings, mind, and phenomena. The seventh factor of the Noble Eightfold Path.
Unified mind developed through the four jhanas. The eighth factor of the Noble Eightfold Path.
Systematic contemplation of body, feelings, mind, and phenomena. The primary framework for insight meditation.
Preventing unarisen unwholesome states, abandoning arisen ones, cultivating unarisen wholesome states, and maintaining arisen ones. The framework for diligence.
Faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom as spiritual capacities. When strengthened, they become the five powers.
The five faculties developed to an unshakeable degree: faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Part of the thirty-seven factors of awakening.
Mindfulness, investigation, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. Mental qualities that lead to awakening when balanced.
Ethics, meditation, and wisdom as the three essential components of Buddhist practice. The comprehensive framework of the path.
Freedom from the bonds of cyclic existence and mental afflictions. Synonymous with nirvana.
Complete knowledge of all phenomena possessed by a fully awakened buddha. The cognitive aspect of full enlightenment.
The ultimate nature of a buddha as the embodiment of truth and emptiness. The first of the three bodies.
The subtle form of a buddha that teaches bodhisattvas in pure lands. The second of the three bodies.
The physical manifestation of a buddha in ordinary realms to teach beings. The third of the three bodies.

term_tibetan: pha rol tu phyin pa bcu
definition: Extended list adding skillful means, vow, power, and knowledge to the six perfections. Emphasized in Theravada and some Mahayana sources.
Taking the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha as protection and guidance. The foundational act of becoming a Buddhist.
Turning away from worldly concerns toward liberation. The initial motivation in the graduated path.
Positive karmic potential accumulated through virtuous actions. Creates favorable conditions for practice and attainment.
Directing accumulated virtue toward enlightenment of all beings. Prevents merit from being exhausted and magnifies its benefit.
Formal expression of spiritual intentions and goals. Shapes the direction of one's practice and future rebirths.
Sacred circular diagram representing the cosmos or deity palace. Used in meditation and ritual in Vajrayana Buddhism.
Sacred syllables or phrases repeated in meditation and ritual. Considered to embody the qualities of buddhas and deities.
Tantric initiation ritual authorizing practice of specific meditation deities and techniques. Essential for Vajrayana practice.
The tantric vehicle of Buddhism using advanced methods to achieve swift enlightenment. Prominent in Tibetan Buddhism.
The Great Vehicle emphasizing the bodhisattva path and universal liberation. Includes Zen, Pure Land, and Tibetan Buddhism.
The School of the Elders, preserving the Pali canon and emphasizing individual liberation. Dominant in Southeast Asia.
East Asian school emphasizing direct pointing to mind-nature through meditation and koans. Known as Chan in Chinese, Seon in Korean.
Complete understanding of reality and liberation from ignorance. The defining achievement of a buddha.
One who has fully awakened to the nature of reality and is freed from all limitations. The highest spiritual attainment.
The Buddha's teachings on the path to liberation and the nature of reality. Also means phenomenon, law, or principle.
Bodhisattva of compassion who perceives the sounds of the world. One of the most popular figures in Mahayana Buddhism.
Bodhisattva of wisdom who wields the sword that cuts through ignorance. Particularly revered in Zen and Tibetan traditions.
The future Buddha who will appear when Shakyamuni's teachings have disappeared. Currently a bodhisattva in Tushita heaven.
Buddha of Infinite Light who presides over Sukhavati pure land. Central figure in Pure Land Buddhism.
Female bodhisattva embodying enlightened activity and swift compassion. Particularly important in Tibetan Buddhism with green and white forms.
The naturally radiant quality of mind underlying mental afflictions. A key concept in Mahayana and tantric Buddhism.
The subtle level of consciousness recognized at death or in advanced meditation. Direct realization of this is enlightenment in highest yoga tantra.
Intermediate state between death and rebirth. Extensively described in Tibetan Buddhism, particularly the Bardo Thodol.
Seventh-century Madhyamaka philosopher who developed the Prasangika approach. His works are authoritative in Tibetan Buddhism.
Eighth-century Indian master who wrote the Bodhicaryavatara (Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life). His work is central to Mahayana ethics.
Successive incarnations of Avalokiteshvara serving as spiritual and temporal leaders of Tibet. The current is the fourteenth.
Physical act of bowing fully to the ground as expression of reverence and purification. A preliminary practice in Tibetan Buddhism.
Ritual walking clockwise around sacred objects or places. A common devotional practice accumulating merit.
Dome-shaped structure containing relics or representing enlightened mind. A focal point for devotion and circumambulation.
Physical remains of buddhas or saints, often taking the form of pearl-like crystals. Objects of veneration and enshrinement.
Place where the historical Buddha passed into parinirvana. One of the four primary Buddhist pilgrimage sites.
Birthplace of the historical Buddha in present-day Nepal. One of the four primary Buddhist pilgrimage sites.
Place where the Buddha achieved enlightenment under the Bodhi tree. The most sacred Buddhist pilgrimage site.
Place where the Buddha gave his first teaching on the four noble truths. One of the four primary Buddhist pilgrimage sites.
Mental construction of images of deities, pure lands, or symbolic forms in meditation. Central technique in Vajrayana practice.
Tantric practice of visualizing oneself as an enlightened deity. Transforms ordinary perception into wisdom awareness.
Practice of merging one's mind with the teacher's enlightened awareness. A preliminary practice generating devotion and blessings.
One's primary spiritual teacher who introduces the nature of mind. The most important relationship in Vajrayana Buddhism.
Succession of teachers transmitting teachings from the Buddha to the present. Ensures authenticity and blessing continuity.
Reading of texts aloud by a qualified teacher to authorize their practice. Maintains unbroken lineage connection.
Essential practical advice pointing directly to meditation techniques. Transmitted privately from teacher to student.
Extended period of intensive practice in seclusion. Traditional retreats last three years, three months, and three days.
Foundation practices including refuge, prostrations, Vajrasattva, mandala offering, and guru yoga. Prepare the mind for advanced tantric practice.
Advanced tantric practices working with subtle energies and consciousness. Follows the generation stage in highest yoga tantra.
Tantric visualization practices creating pure appearance of deity and mandala. The first stage of highest yoga tantra.
System of energy channels, winds, and drops manipulated in tantric practice. Basis for completion stage meditation.
Main energy channel running through the body's center in tantric physiology. Focus of advanced completion stage practices.
Tantric practice generating blissful heat at the navel to melt subtle drops. One of the six yogas of Naropa.
Practice of maintaining awareness during dreams to recognize their illusory nature. One of the six yogas of Naropa.
Realization of one's form as empty appearance during waking state. Advanced completion stage attainment.
Practice of ejecting consciousness at death to ensure favorable rebirth. One of the six yogas of Naropa.
Method of refuting opponents by showing absurd consequences of their positions. Core technique in Prasangika Madhyamaka.
Madhyamaka sub-school using positive logical arguments accepted by both parties. Associated with Bhavaviveka.
Nagarjuna's eight-fold negation of arising, ceasing, permanence, annihilation, coming, going, identity, and difference. Expresses ultimate emptiness.
Relative truth about conventional reality that functions in ordinary experience. Contrasts with ultimate truth in the two truths doctrine.
Highest truth about the ultimate nature of reality as empty. The goal of philosophical analysis in Madhyamaka.
Yogacara analysis: five sense consciousnesses, mental consciousness, afflicted mind, and storehouse consciousness. Comprehensive model of awareness.
Karmic potentials stored in storehouse consciousness that ripen into experiences. Yogacara explanation of karmic continuity.
The fictional nature imposed by conceptual elaboration in Yogacara's three natures. The source of delusion.
The dependent nature of phenomena arising from causes and conditions. The middle nature in Yogacara's three natures.
The perfected nature of reality when imagined nature is removed from dependent nature. The ultimate truth in Yogacara.
Yogacara doctrine that all experience is constructed by consciousness without external objects. Also called mind-only.
The sphere of reality or ultimate nature of phenomena. In Yogacara, the true suchness free from duality.
The true nature of things as they are, beyond conceptual elaboration. Synonymous with emptiness and dharma realm.
Structured liturgical text guiding tantric meditation practice with a deity. Contains visualization, mantra, and offerings.
Hidden teachings concealed by Padmasambhava and revealed by tertons. A distinctive feature of Nyingma tradition.
Master who discovers and reveals concealed teachings in Tibetan Buddhism. Identified through signs and prophecies.
Symbolic hand gestures expressing inner states in tantric practice. Each deity has characteristic mudras.
Ritual implement symbolizing indestructible diamond-like emptiness and compassion. Central symbol in Vajrayana Buddhism.
Female embodiment of wisdom and enlightened energy in tantric Buddhism. Can be mundane or supramundane.
Personal deity chosen for tantric practice representing aspects of enlightenment. Central to deity yoga.
Wrathful deity sworn to protect Buddhist teachings and practitioners. Can be mundane or enlightened.
Tibetan tradition of transforming adversity into the path through cultivation of bodhicitta. Includes tonglen and seven points.
Tantric practice of offering one's body to spirits to cut ego-clinging. Combines Prajnaparamita philosophy with tantric visualization.
Fourteenth-century Nyingma master who systematized Dzogchen teachings. Author of Seven Treasuries and other major works.
Eleventh-century Indian mahasiddha who transmitted six yogas to Marpa. Key figure in Kagyu lineage.
Tenth-century Indian mahasiddha, teacher of Naropa. Received Mahamudra teachings directly from Vajradhara.
Eleventh-century Tibetan translator who studied with Naropa and brought Kagyu teachings to Tibet. Teacher of Milarepa.
Twelfth-century Tibetan master who combined Kadam and Mahamudra traditions. Systematized Kagyu teachings and founded monasteries.
Thirteenth-century Tibetan scholar of Sakya tradition. Renowned for scholarship in Buddhist logic and epistemology.
Fourteenth-century Tibetan master who taught shentong (other-emptiness) view. Founder of Jonang tradition's philosophical approach.
Nineteenth-century Nyingma master and polymath. Wrote extensively on philosophy, tantra, medicine, and astrology.
Nineteenth-century Nyingma master known for simple lifestyle and Words of My Perfect Teacher. Emphasized practice over scholarship.
Nineteenth-century Tibetan master who compiled Five Treasuries. Leader of Rime (non-sectarian) movement.
Twentieth-century Nyingma master known for vast learning and realization. Teacher of many contemporary lamas.
Massive Mahayana sutra teaching interpenetration of all phenomena. Basis of Huayan philosophy.
Mahayana sutra featuring lay bodhisattva Vimalakirti teaching emptiness and non-duality. Emphasizes lay practice.
Yogacara text attributed to Asanga describing bodhisattva stages and practices. Part of Yogacarabhumi collection.
Maitreya's treatise systematizing perfection of wisdom sutras into eight topics. Central to Tibetan monastic curriculum.
Chandrakirti's introduction to Madhyamaka philosophy through ten bodhisattva grounds. Authoritative Prasangika text.

term_tibetan: byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa la 'jug pa
definition: Shantideva's guide to bodhisattva practice emphasizing patience, wisdom, and dedication. One of most beloved Mahayana texts.

term_tibetan: dbu ma rtsa ba'i tshig le'ur byas pa
definition: Nagarjuna's root verses on the Middle Way. Foundational text of Madhyamaka philosophy.
Massive Yogacara encyclopedic text attributed to Asanga. Covers stages of practice and philosophical topics.
Highest yoga tantra text central to Gelug tradition. Teaches generation and completion stage practices.
Highest yoga tantra important in Sakya tradition. Emphasizes non-dual wisdom and bliss.
Highest yoga tantra linking cosmology, astrology, and practice. Known for elaborate initiation and Shambhala connection.
Classic Chan collection of 100 koans with commentary. Central text for Zen koan study.
Collection of 48 Chan koans compiled by Wumen. Includes famous 'Mu' and 'Sound of one hand' koans.
Dogen's masterwork on Zen philosophy and practice. 95 fascicles exploring Buddha-nature, time, and practice-realization.
Zen practice of meditating on paradoxical questions or stories to break through conceptual thinking. Central to Rinzai tradition.
Soto Zen practice of sitting meditation without object or goal. Dogen taught this as practice-realization unity.
Pure Land practice of reciting Amitabha Buddha's name. Cultivates faith and aspiration for rebirth in pure land.
Chan practice of investigating the meaning before words arise. Similar to koan practice but focusing on single phrase.
Chan method of pointing directly to mind's nature beyond words and concepts. Attributed to Bodhidharma's transmission.
The ultimate nature of consciousness as empty, luminous, and unobstructed. Central to Dzogchen and Mahamudra.
Formal walking practice alternating with sitting meditation in Zen. Maintains mindfulness between sitting periods.
Week-long intensive Zen meditation retreat. Combines extended sitting with koan study or shikantaza.
Zen monastic meal ritual performed with nested bowls in silence. Mindfulness practice extending meditation to eating.
Tantric feast offering with food, drink, and ritual substances. Accumulates merit and strengthens commitments.
Chinese meditation school emphasizing direct realization. Became Zen in Japan, Seon in Korea, Thien in Vietnam.
Chinese school based on Lotus Sutra teaching perfect integration of all phenomena. Founded by Zhiyi.
Chinese school based on Avatamsaka Sutra teaching mutual interpenetration. Known for sophisticated metaphysics.
Chinese Madhyamaka school based on Nagarjuna's three treatises. Transmitted by Kumarajiva.
Chinese Yogacara school based on mind-only philosophy. Founded by Xuanzang after studying in India.
Tiantai integration of calming and insight meditation. Simultaneous cultivation rather than sequential stages.
Tiantai teaching that all phenomena perfectly include each other without obstruction. Expresses non-dual reality.
Tiantai teaching of empty, provisional, and middle truths as three aspects of one reality. Expansion of two truths.

term_en: Three Thousand Realms in One Thought
definition: Tiantai doctrine that each moment of consciousness contains all possible states of existence. Expresses totalistic vision.
Huayan teaching that universal principle and particular phenomena interpenetrate freely. Foundation for phenomena-phenomena non-obstruction.
Fully ordained male monastic following complete vinaya. Takes upwards of 250 precepts.
Fully ordained female monastic following complete vinaya. Takes upwards of 300 precepts.
Practitioner following Hinayana path to arhatship by hearing teachings. One of three vehicle types.
The Mahayana path of cultivating enlightenment for all beings through perfections and grounds. Superior to individual liberation.
First basket of Buddhist canon containing monastic rules and procedures. Foundation of sangha organization.
Second basket of Buddhist canon containing Buddha's discourses. Core doctrinal teachings.
Third basket of Buddhist canon containing systematic analysis. Philosophical and psychological elaborations.
The complete Buddhist canon divided into vinaya, sutra, and abhidharma. Foundation of Buddhist literature.
Early Buddhist text collections preserved in Chinese and Pali. Contains Buddha's discourses organized thematically.
Extended mantric formulae that protect and retain teachings. Longer than mantras, used in Mahayana and Vajrayana.
Sustained observation of phenomena in mindfulness practice. Component of four foundations of mindfulness.
Framework of contemplating body, feelings, mind, and phenomena. Primary structure for vipassana practice.
The four immeasurables as sublime states leading to high rebirth. Also called boundless states.
Extended ethical code for novices adding restraint from gold, high beds, entertainment, and eating after noon. Foundation for monastic ordination.
Intention or will that directs mental activity. Key mental factor determining karmic quality of actions.
Mental and physical phenomena in the fourth link of dependent origination. Represents psycho-physical organism.
The twelve bases: six sense faculties and six sense objects. Framework for analyzing perceptual process.
The eighteen elements: six faculties, six objects, six consciousnesses. Complete analysis of perceptual experience.
Confession and purification of negative actions through regret, remedial action, and resolve. Essential preliminary practice.
Action tantra emphasizing external purification and ritual. Lowest of four tantra classes.
Performance tantra balancing external and internal practice. Second of four tantra classes.
Yoga tantra emphasizing internal meditation over ritual. Third of four tantra classes.
Highest tantra class working with subtle body and clear light. Includes generation and completion stages.
The state of complete enlightenment with elimination of all obscurations and perfection of all qualities. Ultimate goal of Mahayana path.
Epithet for buddha meaning 'thus-gone' or 'thus-come.' Indicates realization of suchness.
The four-cornered logic (tetralemma): affirmation, negation, both, neither. Used in Madhyamaka to demonstrate the limits of conceptual thought.
Intrinsic nature or own-being. Madhyamaka denies svabhāva in all phenomena; Abhidharma traditions affirm it for dharmas.
The 'consequentialist' sub-school of Madhyamaka using reductio arguments to expose contradictions without asserting a counter-thesis. Associated with Buddhapālita and Candrakīrti.
The 'autonomist' sub-school of Madhyamaka that uses independent syllogisms to establish emptiness. Associated with Bhāviveka.
A reductio ad absurdum argument showing that an opponent's position leads to unwanted consequences. The primary logical method of Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka.
Conventional designation or worldly transaction. The level of everyday reality acknowledged by Madhyamaka while denying its ultimate existence.
Ultimate reality or highest meaning. In Madhyamaka, the ultimate is the emptiness of inherent existence in all phenomena.
Absence of intrinsic nature. The Madhyamaka thesis that no phenomenon possesses svabhāva, establishing universal emptiness.
Conceptual proliferation or mental elaboration. The tendency of mind to construct and multiply concepts, which Madhyamaka seeks to still.
Illusion or magical display. In Madhyamaka, phenomena appear like illusions—arising dependently yet lacking inherent existence.
Exclusion theory of meaning developed by Dignāga. Words denote by excluding what is not the referent rather than by pointing to a positive entity.
Valid cognition or means of knowledge. Dignāga and Dharmakīrti's Buddhist epistemology recognizes perception and inference as the two valid sources of knowledge.
The three natures (imaginary, dependent, perfected) that constitute Yogācāra's model of reality. Understanding their interrelation leads to awakening.
The storehouse consciousness that holds karmic seeds and underlies experience. A key Yogācāra concept explaining continuity without a permanent self.
Seeds or potencies stored in the ālaya-vijñāna. They ripen under conditions to produce experience, explaining how karma operates across lifetimes.
The imaginary nature—the superimposition of subject-object duality onto experience. What ordinary beings mistake for reality.
The dependent nature—the causal flow of experience arising from conditions. The basis upon which both imaginary and perfected natures operate.
The perfected nature—the dependent nature seen without superimposition. Realized when the imaginary nature is seen through.
In Yogācāra, the seventh consciousness (kliṣṭa-manas) that clings to the ālaya-vijñāna as a self, producing the root affliction of self-grasping.
Consciousness-only or representation-only. The Yogācāra thesis that experienced reality is nothing beyond cognitive representations.
Habitual tendency or latent impression. Residual traces of past actions and experiences stored in the ālaya-vijñāna that condition future experience.
Transformation of the basis—the fundamental revolution in consciousness where the ālaya-vijñāna becomes mirror-like wisdom. The Yogācāra model of enlightenment.
Mental continuum or stream of consciousness. The continuous flow of mental events that provides personal identity without requiring a permanent self.
Treasure texts hidden by Padmasambhava and others for future discovery. Revealed by tertöns when conditions ripen. A distinctive Nyingma institution.
A treasure revealer who discovers hidden terma texts or objects. Important figures in Nyingma lineage transmission.
Oral transmission or reading authorization in Tibetan Buddhism. A formal recitation by a qualified teacher that authorizes a student to study and practice a text.
Empowerment or initiation ceremony that authorizes a practitioner to engage in specific tantric practices. Typically involves body, speech, mind, and wisdom empowerments.
Inner heat yoga, one of the Six Yogas of Nāropa. Generates psychic heat through visualization and breath control to dissolve subtle winds into the central channel.
Consciousness transference practice, one of the Six Yogas of Nāropa. Trains ejection of consciousness at the moment of death to achieve favorable rebirth.
The practice of giving and taking—breathing in suffering of others and breathing out well-being. A core lojong practice for developing bodhicitta.
Mind training through pithy slogans (such as the Seven Points of Mind Training by Atīśa/Chekawa) designed to transform adversity into the path of awakening.
Preliminary practices that prepare a student for advanced tantric meditation. Typically includes 100,000 each of prostrations, Vajrasattva mantras, mandala offerings, and guru yoga.
The Great Seal—the highest meditation practice of the Kagyü lineage. Direct recognition of the nature of mind as empty, luminous, and unimpeded.
A meditational deity with whom a practitioner forms a bond through empowerment. The yidam represents the practitioner's own awakened nature.
A female embodiment of enlightened energy, often appearing as a protector, guide, or consort in Vajrayāna. Literally 'sky-goer.' Yeshe Tsogyal is a famous example.
A recognized incarnation of a deceased Buddhist master, identified through divination and testing. A distinctive Tibetan institution for maintaining lineage continuity.
A ritual offering cake made from barley flour and butter, sculpted into various forms. Used in tantric ceremonies as offerings to deities and protectors.
Sacred commitments undertaken during tantric empowerment. Breaking samaya is considered one of the most serious violations in Vajrayāna.
The three bodies of a buddha: dharmakāya (truth body), saṃbhogakāya (enjoyment body), and nirmāṇakāya (emanation body). Describes how buddhahood manifests at different levels.
The emanation body of a buddha that appears in the world for the benefit of beings. Śākyamuni Buddha's physical form is considered a nirmāṇakāya.
The truth body or reality body of a buddha. The ultimate nature of mind free from all obscurations, identified with emptiness itself.
The enjoyment body of a buddha, visible only to advanced bodhisattvas. Manifests in pure lands as luminous form adorned with the marks and signs of buddhahood.
The Great Perfection—the highest teaching of the Nyingma school. Direct introduction to the nature of mind as primordially pure and spontaneously present.
Cutting through rigidity—the first phase of Dzogchen practice. Direct recognition of the natural state of awareness, primordial purity (ka dag).
Crossing over directly—the second phase of Dzogchen practice. Uses specific postures and gazing to manifest the luminous display of spontaneous presence (lhun grub).
Pure awareness or innate wakefulness in Dzogchen. The fundamental nature of mind that is empty, luminous, and unconfined.
A public case or precedent used in Chan/Zen as a meditation focus. Famous examples include 'What is the sound of one hand clapping?' and 'Zhaozhou's dog.' Known in Japanese as kōan.
Buddha-recollection or Buddha-remembrance. In Chinese Pure Land, the practice of invoking Amitābha Buddha's name (Namo Amituofo) to attain rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
The critical phrase or 'word-head' before a thought arises. A Chan meditation technique focusing on the questioning sensation itself rather than the intellectual content.
Cessation and contemplation—the Tiantai meditation system developed by Zhiyi. Integrates calming (zhǐ) and insight (guān) as inseparable aspects of practice.
Perfect interfusion or mutual containment. A Huayan and Tiantai philosophical principle that all phenomena interpenetrate without obstruction.
The dharma-realm or totality of reality. In Huayan, the universe as an infinite web of mutual interpenetration. Fazang's Four Dharmadhātus are a key doctrinal framework.
Buddha-nature as understood in Chinese Buddhism. The innate capacity for awakening present in all sentient beings. Central to the tathāgatagarbha doctrine in East Asian traditions.

term_tibetan: de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po
definition: The embryo or womb of the Tathāgata—the innate potential for buddhahood within all beings. A major Mahāyāna doctrine bridging emptiness and buddha-nature teachings.
Pure Land—a buddha-field created by a buddha's merit, especially Amitābha's Sukhāvatī. In Chinese/Japanese Pure Land Buddhism, rebirth there is the primary soteriological goal.
The Buddha of Infinite Light who presides over the Western Pure Land (Sukhāvatī). Central to East Asian Pure Land Buddhism. Invoked as 'Namo Amituofo' in Chinese tradition.
Suchness or thusness—reality as it truly is, beyond conceptual elaboration. A key term in Yogācāra and East Asian Buddhism for the unconditioned nature of all phenomena.
Three thousand realms in a single moment of thought. Tiantai doctrine that each moment of consciousness contains all possible states of existence. Expresses Zhiyi's totalistic vision.
Sudden awakening—the Chan/Zen teaching that enlightenment occurs in a single transformative moment rather than through gradual stages. Associated with the Southern School of Huineng.
Gradual awakening—the teaching that enlightenment unfolds through progressive stages of practice and realization. Associated with the Northern School of Shenxiu.
A Chan master—an honorific for recognized Chan/Zen teachers. Famous examples include Huineng, Mazu, Linji, and Zhaozhou.
Mind-nature or the inherent nature of mind. A central concept in Chan Buddhism referring to the original, pure nature of consciousness that is always present.
Vasubandhu's Treasury of Abhidharma. The most influential systematic presentation of Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika philosophy, studied across all Buddhist traditions.
The Path of Purification by Buddhaghosa. The most comprehensive Theravāda meditation manual, systematically covering morality, concentration, and wisdom.

term_tibetan: byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa la 'jug pa
definition: Śāntideva's guide to the bodhisattva path. Celebrated for its ninth chapter on wisdom (prajñā) and its teachings on exchanging self and other.

term_tibetan: dri ma med par grags pa'i bstan pa
definition: The teaching of Vimalakīrti—a Mahāyāna sūtra featuring a lay householder who defeats learned monks in debate. Famous for its 'thunderous silence' on nonduality.
The Stages of the Yoga Practitioner, attributed to Asaṅga/Maitreya. A massive encyclopedic work covering all stages of the path in the Yogācāra tradition.
The Ornament of Clear Realization, attributed to Maitreya. Systematizes the Prajñāpāramitā teachings into eight topics and seventy points.

term_tibetan: chos kyi tshigs su bcad pa
definition: Verses of the Dharma—a collection of 423 verses attributed to the Buddha. One of the most widely read Buddhist texts, included in the Khuddaka Nikāya.
The Questions of Milinda—dialogues between the Indo-Greek king Menander I and the Buddhist monk Nāgasena. Famous for its chariot analogy illustrating non-self.
Liberation Through Hearing in the Intermediate State (Tibetan Book of the Dead). A Nyingma terma text guiding consciousness through the bardo experiences after death.
The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna, attributed to Aśvaghoṣa. Highly influential in East Asian Buddhism for its synthesis of tathāgatagarbha and ālayavijñāna doctrines.
The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom, attributed to Nāgārjuna. A massive commentary preserved only in Chinese translation (Kumārajīva). Encyclopedic resource on Mahāyāna.
Loving-kindness—the wish for all beings to be happy. One of the four brahma-vihāras. Cultivated through systematic meditation extending goodwill to self, loved ones, neutrals, and enemies.
Compassion—the wish for all beings to be free from suffering. A brahma-vihāra and the heart of the bodhisattva path. Mahākaruṇā (great compassion) is a defining quality of buddhahood.
Sympathetic joy—rejoicing in others' happiness and success. One of the four brahma-vihāras. Antidote to jealousy and envy.
Equanimity—even-minded balance toward all beings and experiences. One of the four brahma-vihāras. Not indifference but impartial care.

term_tibetan: dran pa nye bar gzhag pa
definition: The four foundations of mindfulness: body, feelings, mind, and mental objects. The Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta is considered the most important meditation instruction in the Pali Canon.

term_tibetan: dbugs rngub pa dang 'byung ba dran pa
definition: Mindfulness of breathing—a foundational meditation practice taught by the Buddha. The sixteen steps of ānāpānasati progress from bodily awareness through to liberation.

Higher knowledge or supranormal powers attained through deep concentration. Traditionally six: divine eye, divine ear, mind-reading, recollection of past lives, psychic powers, and destruction of āsravas.
Ethical discipline or moral conduct. The first of the three trainings (along with samādhi and prajñā). Foundation of the Buddhist path, ranging from five precepts to full monastic vinaya.
Meditative absorption or concentration. The second of the three trainings. One-pointed focus of mind ranging from access concentration to the formless attainments.
Wisdom or insight—direct understanding of the nature of reality. The third of the three trainings and the sixth pāramitā. Prajñāpāramitā (perfection of wisdom) is central to Mahāyāna.
The reality-realm or expanse of phenomena. In Huayan, the infinite interpenetration of all dharmas. In Yogācāra, the purified nature of reality.
Person or individual. The Pudgalavāda school controversially affirmed a 'person' that is neither identical to nor different from the aggregates, sparking major philosophical debate.
The nature of phenomena or reality as it is. In Dzogchen, the dharmata bardo is the period after death when reality's nature manifests directly.
Cognitive object or object of mental focus. In Yogācāra epistemology, the question of whether ālambana can be external to consciousness is central.
Cause and condition—the two factors that produce all conditioned phenomena. Detailed analysis of causation is fundamental to Abhidharma philosophy.
Volitional formations or mental constructions. The fourth aggregate and second link of dependent origination. The karmic force that shapes future experience.
Mental afflictions or defilements—the root causes of suffering. Primary kleśas include desire, aversion, and ignorance. Their elimination is the goal of the Buddhist path.
Obscuration or obstruction. Mahāyāna identifies two: kleśāvaraṇa (afflictive obscurations) and jñeyāvaraṇa (cognitive obscurations). Buddhahood requires removing both.
Stage or ground on the bodhisattva path. The Daśabhūmika Sūtra describes ten bhūmis from Joyful to Cloud of Dharma, each characterized by specific realizations and practices.
Spiritual lineage or family determining one's capacity for awakening. Yogācāra distinguishes five gotras. The question of whether all beings possess buddha-gotra is a major doctrinal debate.
Skill in means—a buddha or bodhisattva's ability to adapt teachings to the capacities and circumstances of beings. Justifies the diversity of Buddhist methods and vehicles.
The great Kuchean-Indian translator (344-413 CE) who rendered major Mahāyāna texts into Chinese. His translations of the Heart Sūtra, Lotus Sūtra, and Mādhyamaka texts shaped East Asian Buddhism.
Chinese Buddhist monk (602-664 CE) who traveled to India and brought back hundreds of texts. His translations founded the Faxiang (Yogācāra) school in China. Subject of Journey to the West.
The de facto founder of the Tiantai school (538-597 CE). Systematized Buddhist doctrine through the panjiao classification and developed the zhǐguān meditation system.
The third patriarch and systematizer of the Huayan school (643-712 CE). Developed the doctrine of the four dharmadhātus and the famous gold lion metaphor for interpenetration.
The Sixth Patriarch of Chan Buddhism (638-713 CE). His Platform Sūtra advocates sudden awakening and is the only Chinese-authored text honored with the title 'sūtra.'
Influential Tang dynasty Chan master (709-788 CE). Famous for shocking teaching methods and the declaration 'this mind is Buddha.' His lineage produced many of Chan's greatest masters.
Founder of the Linji (Rinzai) school of Chan (d. 866 CE). Known for his 'four shouts' and fierce teaching style. His recorded sayings (Línjì Lù) are a classic of Chan literature.
Japanese founder of Sōtō Zen (1200-1253 CE). His Shōbōgenzō is a masterwork of Buddhist philosophy. Emphasized shikantaza (just sitting) as the practice of enlightenment itself.
The Land of Ultimate Bliss—Amitābha Buddha's western pure land. Described in the Longer and Shorter Sukhāvatīvyūha sūtras. Primary goal of Pure Land devotion.
A wheel-turning monarch who rules justly over the world. In Buddhist cosmology, a being of immense merit who may choose either worldly sovereignty or buddhahood.
The axial mountain at the center of Buddhist cosmology. Surrounded by concentric rings of mountains and oceans, with the heavens above and hells below.
The individual liberation code of monastic rules recited fortnightly. Contains 227 rules for bhikkhus in Theravāda and 250 in the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition.
The twelve links of dependent origination: ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, aging-and-death.
Outflows, taints, or cankers. Three or four mental defilements (sensual desire, existence, ignorance, and sometimes views) whose destruction marks the attainment of arhatship.
The seat or place of awakening—originally the spot under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya where Siddhārtha became the Buddha. Also used metaphorically for any place of practice.
A reliquary monument housing the remains or relics of a buddha or saint. A focus of devotion and circumambulation. Architecture varies from Indian dome to East Asian pagoda forms.
A Buddhist monastery or dwelling place for monks. Originally simple rain retreats, they developed into major centers of learning. Nālandā and Vikramaśīla were famous vihāras.
A fully ordained Buddhist nun. The bhikṣuṇī saṅgha was established by the Buddha at the request of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. The lineage continues in East Asian traditions.
Clear light or luminosity practice, one of the Six Yogas of Nāropa. Recognition of the nature of mind in the dream state and at death as luminous awareness.
Dream yoga, one of the Six Yogas of Nāropa. Training in lucid dreaming to recognize the illusory nature of experience, preparing for bardo recognition at death.
Illusory body practice, one of the Six Yogas of Nāropa. Cultivating the understanding that the body is like an illusion, ultimately transforming it into the pure illusory body.
Perfection or transcendent virtue. The six (or ten) pāramitās are the bodhisattva's path: generosity, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom.
A mnemonic formula, incantation, or sustained attention. Longer and more content-bearing than mantras, dhāraṇīs are used for protection, purification, and generating merit.

term_tibetan: byang chub kyi phyogs kyi chos
definition: The 37 factors of awakening: four foundations of mindfulness, four right efforts, four bases of power, five faculties, five powers, seven factors of awakening, and the noble eightfold path.
A buddha-field or buddha-land. Each buddha's sphere of influence where beings can be taught. Mahāyāna describes infinite buddha-fields across space and time.
Aspiration or vow. A bodhisattva's formal resolve directing future lifetimes toward benefiting beings. Amitābha's 48 vows and Samantabhadra's 10 vows are famous examples.
Meditative absorption. Four form-realm dhyānas progress from applied thought to equanimity. The Chinese term chán (禪) derives from this word.

term_tibetan: bla na med pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i byang chub
definition: Unsurpassed complete perfect awakening—the full enlightenment of a buddha. Distinguished from the awakening of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Well-gone or happily departed—an epithet of the Buddha indicating one who has gone to the excellent state and will not return to saṃsāra.
